A job is a unit of work submitted to the system for execution — in classical batch systems, a user's program together with its data and its control statements (JCL cards) handed over as one package. A process is a program in execution: an active entity with a program counter, a stack, a data section, and a set of resources allocated to it by the operating system.

The distinction comes from batch processing. A job is the unit handled by the long-term scheduler (the job scheduler), which selects jobs from the job pool held on disk and admits them into main memory. Once admitted, the job becomes one or more processes, and the short-term scheduler (the CPU scheduler) then multiplexes the CPU among those ready processes.

So a job is passive and static — a description of work waiting in a queue, with no execution state. A process is dynamic: it has a state (new, ready, running, waiting, terminated), a Process Control Block holding its registers and accounting data, and it can create child processes. One job may give rise to several processes; a process cannot exist without a program being run.

Galvin notes the two terms are now used almost interchangeably, since interactive systems have largely displaced batch jobs and both schedulers do the same kind of work.
points: Defines a job as a unit of work submitted for execution (program + data + control statements), passive and static
Defines a process as a program in execution — an active entity with PC, stack, data section and allocated resources
States that the long-term (job) scheduler admits jobs from the job pool; the short-term (CPU) scheduler dispatches processes
States that one job can give rise to several processes
Mentions that a process has state (new/ready/running/waiting/terminated) and a PCB, which a job does not
Notes that the terms are largely historical and are now used interchangeably in modern texts

Multiprogramming keeps several programs resident in main memory at the same time on a single CPU. When the running process blocks for I/O, the operating system switches the CPU to another process that is ready, so the CPU is never left idle while I/O proceeds. Its goal is to maximise CPU utilisation and throughput. Only one process is actually executing at any given instant — the parallelism is apparent (interleaved), not real.

Multiprocessing means the system contains two or more physical CPUs or cores, sharing the bus, memory and peripheral devices under the control of one operating system. Two or more processes genuinely execute at the same instant, so the parallelism is real. Its goals are increased throughput, economy of scale (sharing peripherals and memory), and increased reliability through graceful degradation — the system keeps running when one processor fails.

Key differences: number of CPUs (one versus many); nature of parallelism (interleaved versus simultaneous); hardware cost (low versus high); and OS complexity — a multiprocessor must handle processor scheduling, cache coherence and inter-processor synchronisation, whereas multiprogramming needs only memory protection and CPU scheduling.

The two are orthogonal, not alternatives: a multiprocessor system is normally also multiprogrammed. The usual organisation is symmetric multiprocessing (SMP), where every processor runs an identical copy of the OS.
points: Multiprogramming = several programs in memory, one CPU, switch on I/O wait; parallelism is apparent/interleaved
Multiprocessing = two or more physical CPUs under one OS; parallelism is real/simultaneous
States the goal of multiprogramming is CPU utilisation and throughput
States the goals of multiprocessing: increased throughput, economy of scale, increased reliability (graceful degradation)
Notes multiprocessing needs cache coherence and inter-processor synchronisation, adding OS complexity
Notes the two are orthogonal — a multiprocessor system is usually also multiprogrammed (SMP)

Deadlock avoidance requires each process to declare in advance the maximum number of resources of each type it may ever need; the system then grants a request only if doing so leaves the system in a safe state. The standard method is Dijkstra's Banker's algorithm, which works for multiple instances of each resource type.

Data structures for n processes and m resource types: Available[m], Max[n][m], Allocation[n][m], and Need[n][m] = Max - Allocation.

A state is safe if a safe sequence <P1, ..., Pn> exists such that each Pi's remaining Need can be met by the currently Available resources plus those held by all Pj before it — every process can finish in turn.

Safety algorithm: set Work = Available and Finish[i] = false for all i. Find any i with Finish[i] = false and Need[i] <= Work; if found, set Work = Work + Allocation[i], Finish[i] = true, and repeat. If every Finish[i] becomes true, the state is safe.

Resource-request algorithm: when Pi requests Request[i], check Request[i] <= Need[i] and Request[i] <= Available. If both hold, tentatively allocate (Available -= Request, Allocation[i] += Request, Need[i] -= Request) and run the safety algorithm. If the trial state is safe the allocation stands; otherwise Pi waits and the old state is restored.

Note an unsafe state is not necessarily a deadlock — avoidance is conservative and simply refuses to enter one.
points: Names Banker's algorithm and states its precondition: each process declares its maximum resource need in advance
Lists the data structures Available, Max, Allocation and Need = Max - Allocation
Correctly defines a safe state / safe sequence
States the safety algorithm: Work = Available, find Need[i] <= Work, Work += Allocation[i], repeat until all Finish[i] true
States the resource-request algorithm: check Request <= Need and Request <= Available, tentatively allocate, test safety, roll back if unsafe
Notes an unsafe state is not the same as a deadlock — avoidance is conservative

In priority scheduling each process is associated with an integer priority, and the CPU is allocated to the ready process with the highest priority. Equal-priority processes are scheduled FCFS. Following Galvin's convention, a smaller number denotes a higher priority.

Priorities may be internal — computed by the OS from measurable quantities such as time limits, memory requirements, or the ratio of average I/O burst to average CPU burst — or external, set from outside the OS on grounds such as the importance of the user, funds paid, or political factors.

There are two variants. In preemptive priority scheduling, a newly arrived process whose priority is higher than that of the running process immediately takes the CPU away from it. In non-preemptive priority scheduling, the new process is merely put at the head of the ready queue and the running process finishes its CPU burst.

SJF is a special case of priority scheduling in which the priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst length.

The major problem is indefinite blocking, or starvation: a low-priority process may wait forever while a steady stream of higher-priority processes keeps arriving. The standard solution is aging — gradually raising the priority of any process that has waited a long time, so it eventually reaches the top of the queue. A related hazard, priority inversion, is handled by the priority-inheritance protocol.
points: States the rule: CPU goes to the highest-priority ready process, ties broken FCFS; smaller number = higher priority (Galvin convention)
Distinguishes internal priorities (computed from time limits, memory, I/O-to-CPU burst ratio) from external ones
Describes both preemptive and non-preemptive variants correctly
States that SJF is priority scheduling with priority = inverse of the predicted next CPU burst
Identifies starvation / indefinite blocking as the main drawback
Gives aging as the remedy (and mentions priority inversion / priority inheritance)

LRU (Least Recently Used) replacement selects for eviction the page that has not been used for the longest period of time. It approximates the optimal (OPT / Belady) algorithm by using the recent past as a predictor of the near future: OPT looks forward along the reference string, LRU looks backward over the same string.

Example, reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 with three frames:

7 fault [7]; 0 fault [7,0]; 1 fault [7,0,1]; 2 fault, replace 7 as least recently used, [2,0,1]; 0 hit; 3 fault, replace 1, [2,0,3]; 0 hit; 4 fault, replace 2, [4,0,3]. Six page faults.

Two hardware implementations are standard. Counters: the CPU keeps a logical clock incremented on every memory reference, and the clock value is copied into the page-table entry of the page referenced; the page with the smallest value is replaced, which requires searching the page table on every fault. Stack: page numbers are held in a doubly linked list, and each referenced page is removed and placed on top; the bottom of the stack is always the LRU page, so no search is needed, though each reference costs several pointer updates.

LRU is a stack algorithm, so it never suffers Belady's anomaly. True LRU needs hardware support, so real systems use approximations such as the second-chance (clock) algorithm based on reference bits.
points: States the rule: replace the page that has not been used for the longest time; LRU looks backward where OPT looks forward
Traces a worked reference string showing which page is evicted at each fault
Describes the counter implementation (logical clock stamped into the page-table entry, smallest value replaced)
Describes the stack implementation (doubly linked list, referenced page moved to top, bottom is LRU, no search needed)
States that LRU is a stack algorithm and therefore free of Belady's anomaly
Notes that true LRU needs hardware support, so second-chance/clock using reference bits is used in practice

SCAN, the elevator algorithm, moves the disk arm steadily in one direction servicing every request it passes, continues to the end of the disk, then reverses and services the requests lying in the other direction on the return sweep.

Given: 200 cylinders numbered 0-199, head at cylinder 100, moving toward 0. Pending requests: 23, 89, 132, 42, 187.

Moving inward from 100 the head meets 89, then 42, then 23. Standard SCAN then continues on to cylinder 0 — the physical end of the disk — before reversing; it does not turn around at the last request. (Turning at the last request is the LOOK variant, not SCAN.) It then sweeps outward and services 132, then 187.

Service order: 89, 42, 23, (0), 132, 187.

Total head movement:

Inward leg: 100 - 0 = 100 cylinders

Outward leg: 187 - 0 = 187 cylinders

Total = 100 + 187 = 287 cylinders.

The question asks for "total time", but no seek rate, rotational latency or transfer time is printed with it, so the answer can only be given as total head movement — 287 cylinders. If a per-cylinder seek time t were supplied, total seek time = 287t.

For comparison, LOOK on the same queue reverses at 23 and gives (100 - 23) + (187 - 23) = 77 + 164 = 241 cylinders.
points: States the SCAN service order: 89, 42, 23, then 0, then 132, 187
States explicitly that standard SCAN travels to cylinder 0 before reversing, and that stopping at 23 would be LOOK
Shows the sum: inward 100 - 0 = 100, outward 187 - 0 = 187
Gives total head movement = 287 cylinders
Names what is missing: no seek rate is printed, so 'time' can only be expressed as head movement (287t if t per cylinder given)
Optional comparison: LOOK gives 77 + 164 = 241 cylinders

A file is a named collection of related information recorded on secondary storage. It is the logical storage unit the user sees — the smallest allotment of named storage the operating system permits a user to create — and the OS maps it onto physical devices, so the user need not know about tracks, sectors or blocks. Typical attributes held in the directory entry are name, identifier, type, location, size, protection, and time, date and owner information. The basic operations are create, write, read, reposition (seek), delete and truncate.

Files are organised at two levels, and the question can be read either way, so both are given.

Organisation of records within a file: sequential — records stored and retrieved strictly in order, cheap and suited to batch processing; indexed sequential (ISAM) — sequentially stored records plus an index of keys, allowing direct access as well; direct or hashed — the record key is hashed to a relative block address, giving the fastest access to a single record but poor sequential retrieval.

Organisation of files within the system (directory structure): single-level; two-level, one directory per user; tree-structured, with subdirectories and absolute or relative path names; acyclic-graph, allowing shared subdirectories via links; and general-graph, which needs cycle detection and garbage collection on deletion.

The access methods built on these are sequential access, direct (relative) access, and index-based access.
points: Defines a file as a named collection of related information on secondary storage — the logical storage unit
Lists file attributes (name, identifier, type, location, size, protection, time/date/owner) and the six basic operations
Gives record-level file organisation: sequential, indexed sequential (ISAM), direct/hashed, with the trade-off of each
Gives system-level organisation via directory structures: single-level, two-level, tree, acyclic-graph, general-graph
Notes general-graph directories require cycle detection / garbage collection
Names the access methods: sequential, direct (relative) and index-based
